speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MOTION FOR REVIEW BY SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I can assure the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River that he need have no qualms on that point. I do not intend to speak for long, and I can also assure him that even if I did say here what I intended to say to the ladies, it would not shock him.
The reason I should appreciate the opportunity of saying a few words now is that I should like, first of all, to express my appreciation to my hon. friend from Parry Sound-Muskoka for having put this subject down on the order paper. I hope he will understand that my action in announcing, a few days earlier than his motion actually appeared, that a special committee on juvenile delinquency was to be set up was not intended in any way to steal his thunder. It is, rather, that the persons concerned with this subject have arrived at the same conclusion, namely, that it is necessary that a concentrated and co-ordinated effort should be made to come to grips with this problem of juvenile delinquency. It is for this reason that I announced earlier in the session the appointment of a special committee within my department to look into all aspects of this matter and to study it across Canada in consultation with other government and private organizations concerned with this field so as to make recommendations within a year as to efforts which may be made by the government, both within its own jurisdiction and in co-operation with other authorities, to improve the situation.
I should like to take this opportunity to correct one impression-one criticism, I should say-which appears to be widespread. A number of organizations wrote to me after the appointment of the committee was announced expressing regret that we had not included upon it any trained social workers. The answer, as I have indicated in my letters on this subject, is that we do not have in my department, for reasons which I think


will be obvious, anyone who has had experience as a trained social worker. I wanted a departmental committee because it was the experience, certainly in connection with the correction and reform program which we instituted, that effective and concentrated work could be done by a departmental committee of this sort. I think, with due respect, in the kind of field in which we are operating more effective, more concentrated and more speedy work can be done by a departmental committee of this sort than by other kinds of general committees or commissions. That was the reason that led us to decide to appoint a departmental committee.
I can assure the house, as I have assured all those who have written me, that there need be no cause for concern that the views of those concerned in this field of social work will not be fully in mind when the committee's report is submitted, when its recommendations to me are prepared, because we have taken care in the terms of reference, the detailed instructions as it were which we gave the committee forming the basis of their operations, to specify that they seek at an early stage meetings and conferences with organizations, welfare societies and individuals active in this field all across Canada for the specific purpose of enabling them to have a first hand and extensive knowledge of the views and recommendations which those concerned with and working in this field would wish to bring to our attention with respect to the solutions and the actions which will be brought to bear on this problem.
It is, as I have said, the intention incorporated in the instructions to the committee that they shall complete their work and let me have a report within a year from the date of their appointment. They are hard at work now. They have made a number of visits to points outside Ottawa. I am glad to be able to report to the house that everywhere they have been in contact with both government and private organizations their presence has been welcomed and the fullest co-operation and mutual interest in arriving at a solution has been evident on the part of those with whom they have met and held their discussions. So I am satisfied that the committee is at work effectively, and I look forward to a useful and constructive report.
The only other observation of a general nature I wish to make at this time is that a certain amount of research, I believe, will be necessary to be done by this committee and by others with whom they work because it has been my conclusion, as a result of the consideration we have given to the matter to date, that there are almost as many impressions of and definitions of the problem

of juvenile delinquency and what constitutes a juvenile delinquent as there are individuals who are called upon to express their opinion. What is a delinquent? What is the age at which a person ceases to be a juvenile delinquent and becomes an adult criminal? These and a host of related problems are questions to which there is no agreed answer, questions on which there has been, in my view, not sufficient attempt as yet to arrive at a common basis of understanding that would be acceptable across Canada, at least as the basis upon which to found an attack upon the problem.
It has always seemed to me that you will not make an effective attack on a problem unless you first of all define clearly and concisely the nature and extent of the problem you wish to cure. This will be one aspect and perhaps the first aspect of the committee's work, to define the nature and extent of the problem of juvenile delinquency in Canada and then to grapple with the question of its basic causes. And then if, as I hope, they are able to come forward with specific answers in those general fields, we should be able to get really concrete and constructive proposals for the cure of the problem.
Recognizing always, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka, that this field is one of divided jurisdiction, I would therefore wish to make it clear that we as a federal government cannot come up with a course of action which will provide the entire solution. We may be able to, and indeed I believe we shall be able to, arrive at a series of recommendations which will cover the whole field, but it will be the case that we as a federal government, under the present constitutional division of responsibility, will be able to act or intervene directly on only a portion of those subjects or perhaps of those recommendations. With respect to the remainder, it will be our intention and our objective so to conduct our own affairs here and so to co-ordinate our own activities that solutions may be found. For instance, I have in mind the activities of the Department of National Health and Welfare, for one thing, and the possibility of the grants in aid for physical fitness; that is one head that occurs to me. Then we would offer a series of coordinated activities or programs with provincial governments and with such other agencies of the provincial governments as they may care to bring to bear on the field, and in so far as lies within our competence, also with private agencies working in this field.
In other words, what it is essential to bear in mind is that the solution is not going to lie in action at one level only. We hope that our
Juvenile Delinquents Act recommendations which will have been discussed in advance with all those across Canada in that field, both governmental and private agencies, will commend themselves to those bodies, and that then we will be able, by action in our field and by co-ordinating where we can do so our activities with others not members of the federal government or its agencies, to accomplish a complete attack on the problem of juvenile delinquency.
Why have we been so concerned as to set up this special study recognizing as we do the complex nature of it to which I have just referred? In brief, the answer to that question is simple, but I believe fundamental. It is that no program designed to meet the problem of and the concern for criminality in Canada can be practical or complete unless it attacks that problem in all its aspects.
We have attacked it at one end with respect to our penitentiary system. We have, we believe, fairly launched an up to date, sensible and sound correctional reform program. We are revising our penal system and the programs operating therein in order that we may have, and I believe we will have, one of the best penitentiary systems in the world. That is only going to be a very partial answer to the problem if we stop there because we would be dealing only with one end of the problem of criminality. If we are going to have a well rounded and complete program it is essential that we deal also with the basic causes and factors which contribute to criminality.
I would think there would be general agreement in this house, at any rate, that one of the first places to start in dealing with the problem of criminals and criminality is to do what you can to prevent people from becoming criminals; and surely you can take no more effective action in that field than by launching an attack on the problem of juvenile delinquency. That will be most effectively done on the basis of the following approach, that we give consideration to the young people of this country, even those who may have inherently some psychological or other tendencies which are such that they are prone to become criminals or to fall into a life of delinquency and crime. Then if we can isolate them, find them before they have gone too far down the road, and bring to bear a program such as the one I have hinted at in broad general outline, then we can, I think, confidently expect that we shall have gone a fair way toward preventing the incipient delinquent from becoming a hardened criminal. This is, at any rate, the objective. It is for this reason that we in our department, with the support of my colleagues in the government, have come to the conclusion that, having got our correctional

As I said, I shall bring to the attention of the committee and I myself shall study carefully the remarks made by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka and the remarks which will be made by all those who will speak here in the course of this debate. I thank the hon. member particularly for making it possible to discuss this matter here. I look forward with anticipation to reading the remarks of those who will participate. I should like to express in anticipation my appreciation of the help I am sure we shall derive from them in these sittings.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like first of all to congratulate the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) for having thought of giving the house the opportunity to examine a problem which has become crucial, as anyone who has taken the time to consider the effects of juvenile delinquency in Canada will agree.
I think hon. members appreciate the explanations the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) has given and the additional remarks he has made concerning the work of the committee which was set up to examine precisely the problem of juvenile delinquency and to make all possible and necessary reforms so that we may at least find a partial solution to that problem.
The hon. member who introduced this motion mentioned certain advantages of the present legislation which is to be found in chapter 160 of the Revised Statutes of Canada.
When this legislation was first adopted, the situation was just as serious as it is today. If one reads each article of the act, one comes readily to the conclusion that the role assigned to the state is and must remain that of a substitute and that the heart of the matter is to be found within the family circle, from which stems the problem of juvenile delinquency.
During the 15 years I have been practising law, I have been called many times to appear before the social welfare court to assist young delinquents who had got in trouble

with the law. Much as I hate to admit it, the parents, in almost the majority of cases, had been remiss in their duties, by failing to watch over their children, by not showing enough interest in them and, above all, by too often setting a bad example.
I think the act should not be amended, but it should be more strictly enforced. One has but to read section 33 to see what forceful provisions are laid down concerning parents.
Parents who, through indifference or bad example, allow their growing child to become a juvenile delinquent should be brought before the courts, so that the sentence imposed could serve to remind each and every parent that he is duty bound to try to bring up his children in such a way that they will become worthy members of tomorrow's society.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to commend the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka. I wholeheartedly agree with his remarks concerning the provisions of section 27 of the act.
I think our small towns and municipalities should make it a point of honour to set up a committee of citizens with a view to checking juvenile delinquency within their own territory.
If those who belong to welfare agencies, such as the Rotary, Kiwanis, Richelieu or Knights of Columbus clubs, or other similar organizations, dealt with the real problem of juvenile delinquency, they could do a wonderful job to stem that growing calamity.
Alas. It is often said that juvenile delinquency is but the doorway to crime. I think parents should more often be held responsible for offences committed by their children. When they have been advised that their children must appear before a welfare court, as provided in section 20 of the act, I think that our judges should penalize those parents when there has been real neglect on their part, because, too often, unfortunately, the children only follow the example and advice, especially the example, their parents give them.
While waiting for the committee's report and the adoption of the legislative measures that will undoubtedly be called for later, I think that our welfare courts should be more concerned with the consequences of juvenile delinquency, and the presidents of our courts should see to it more often that the parents are held responsible for their children's misdeeds, when they have shown themselves indifferent and neglectful.

Of course, there are exceptions. Very often, the offences of the children are committed without the knowledge of the parents, but when the latter neglect their duty or set a bad example, I think we should not penalize only the children but rather and especially the parents who are responsible for the crimes committed by those children.
Mr. Speaker, I must somewhat disagree with the mover of the resolution when he says that it would be advantageous for us to give greater publicity to trials that take place before our social welfare courts.
I prefer to endorse the proposal made by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Broome) who, by a bill introduced in this house last year, requested the destruction of young delinquents' files after five years, in order that they be spared the burden and consequences of a criminal record all their lives. I rather think we should give publicity to trials of adults who are brought before our social welfare courts and keep on considering with pity and helping young delinquents, because the prime object of the act is precisely to reform the child who is in trouble.
Section 3 of the Juvenile Delinquents Act shows the real spirit behind the adoption of chapter 160. Section 3, paragraph 2 provides as follows:
Where a child is adjudged to have committed a delinquency he shall be dealt with, not as an offender, but as one in the condition of delinquency and therefore requiring help, guidance and proper supervision.
That, Mr. Speaker, is the role of the father and the mother. As I said a moment ago, if we had the courage of assuming our responsibilities, the state would not invade that field of education, because the Juvenile Delinquents Act aims, first of all, to help and bring back on the right path those of our children who have strayed away from it. If all parents understood the gravity of their task, we would not have to consider today such a serious problem.
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that we all realize how serious is this problem. Therefore let us all try to improve the situation.

I think it would be well for us in this chamber to remember that Canada is not alone in facing this problem. If we read newspapers and magazines we are aware that the problem is faced to an even greater degree in some ways by our friends to the south in the United States. It is certainly also one which the Soviet Union faces and one which causes great concern and consternation in the United Kingdom. Why? There are a great many reasons. Possibly one is the feeling of insecurity in a very insecure age. We are living in an age of transition, of moving from one set of values to another. We are living in a society in


my opinion in which, incidentally, all values are being questioned, and we are living, of course, in a society in which life itself seems to be a very uncertain thing.

The house resumed consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Churchill-Mr. MacEwan in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Veterans' Land Act to extend the period during which a veteran may qualify for benefits; to establish dates on which persons shall be deemed to be discharged; to extend the repayment period of loans; to enable the director to arrange group life insurance for veterans on a voluntary basis; to increase the rate of interest where a property reverts to the director; to increase the maximum assistance under part II; to provide further financial assistance to certain full time farmers; to provide further financial assistance to part time farmers and commercial fishermen; to extend the purposes for which a part III loan may be used; to extend the uses to which proceeds of a sale or other disposition of land may be put; and to provide for the release to a veteran of a portion of the land on which he is established.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO EXTEND QUALIFICATION PERIOD, ETC.
speechtext:
I feel compelled to say a few words on this resolution for more than one reason. First of all, I have been closely associated with this legislation for several years. Second, as one of the "backest" of the back benchers-and I sometimes wonder, in this position, how far our voices carry-I ask myself whether the proposed resolution coincides by accident with some of the suggestions I have made or whether some of my suggestions and recommendations to the minister have played a part in the drafting of the resolution which is before us. It is hard to say.
In any event, it is certainly a source of satisfaction to me to know that many of the provisions in this resolution are such as I have recommended to the minister and to the staff of his department. First, as to the extension of the deadline date. The deadline has, up to now, for all practical purposes, been September, 1962. It has now been extended to October 31, 1968. This action was very necessary because of the many anomalies and inequities which arise in legislation such as this in connection with a deadline. For example, under the provisions which have existed up to the present time, certain veterans would have been eligible after the deadline date whereas others, with overseas service, might have lost their eligibility as of September of this year. Another important factor concerning the extension of the deadline in so far as people now serving in the

armed forces are concerned is this: not too many of them are aware of the fact that they are eligible under at least two parts of the Veterans' Land Act. The first is part II, under which members of the armed forces are eligible, provided a commanding officer can state that they will be stationed in one location for a period of 18 months. Another area of the act with respect to which members of the armed forces generally are not aware of their eligibility includes parts I and III. By virtue of an amendment brought in by the present government, members of the armed forces are eligible under parts I and III of the act, provided they are on their last posting. This extension of the deadline date to 1968 will make available the benefits of this legislation to members of the armed forces for a period of some five years. I should like to have recommended to the government that no tailgate or deadline be included in this legislation. However, we know that this government will still be here to extend the deadline further in 1968 and I take it, therefore, that the present provision will be satisfactory to the veterans of Canada.
Some of the provisions in this resolution are far reaching. The minister had indicated that the amount of loans to small holders will be increased from $10,000 to $12,000. This is particularly significant when we consider that the amount of the increased deposit required to get this larger loan will be only $200. In other words, for a $200 increase in the down payment the loan under part III will be increased from $10,000 to $12,000. This in itself will be most acceptable. But the one new departure indicated in this resolution is the fact that these increased loans, for the first time in the history of the Veterans' Land Act, will be made retroactive. Hitherto, all the increases, first, from $6,000 to $8,000, and then from $8,000 to $10,000, were available only to new borrowers. They were never made available to those veterans who had previously obtained assistance under the act.
As the minister told the committee this afternoon it is now considered that those veterans who are already established should be able to obtain the additional money required to enlarge their homes or their holdings. It is true they might have been able to do this under part IV of the National Housing Act. Over the years I have maintained that the veterans of Canada are deserving of better assistance than is provided under part IV of the housing act, so I think it is one of the satisfactory features of this resolution that all these veterans, numbering in the order of 60,000, established under parts I and
Veterans' Land Act
III of the Veterans' Land Act will now be able to get this additional assistance.
One of the major departures envisaged by this resolution, as I gathered from the minister this afternoon, is the new clause proposed to amend the act in relation to the small family farm. Before I discuss that clause I wonder whether for the sake of clarity and getting the record straight I should refer to the welcome comments made this afternoon by the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo. He read at some length from the report made by the veterans land administration on some 5,000 farmer veterans across Canada, going back to 1957. I think the hon. member did not clearly understand that the recommendations resulting from the findings of that report were fully implemented by this government in 1959. That report indicated the need for additional credit to enable these veterans to set up economic farm units across Canada under the Veterans' Land Act. The act was amended, and those recommendations were implemented by the present section 64 of the act which allows for a loan of up to $20,000 for one farmer, provided he farms an economic unit. That is the crux of the difference between that wonderful legislation and this new proposal mentioned by the minister today, that is, the provision for the small family farm.
The new proposal makes provision for veterans who operate small farms who could not have been accommodated under the existing legislation. Under the small holdings provisions a man was supposed to be able to assure the administration that he had an income from employment and there was a provision relating to the farm being an economic unit before one could qualify for a loan of $20,000. Between these two positions were a large number of veterans operating small family farms who will be taken care of under the new provision.
I think this is a rather bold experiment.
I	hope it will serve as a guinea pig for similar legislation which will be made available to non-veterans who operate small family farms just as the Veterans' Land Act served as a guinea pig for the Farm Credit Act. In the same way I hope this legislation will serve as an experiment for similar legislation to assist non-veterans who operate small family farms.
Another proposed amendment will have the effect of extending the advance under part
II	of the Veterans' Land Act from $10,000 to $12,000. As hon. members no doubt appreciate part II of the act is an adaptation of the National Housing Act to the specific use of veterans. This is part of the self-help program. It must be understood that although the advance is increased from $10,000 to $12,000 the

Canadian Wheat Board Act amount of the loan available to veterans under part II of the act remains the same as it is now under the National Housing Act. In other words for a three bedroom house a veteran under part II can still obtain a loan of $14,200 and for a four bedroom house he may obtain a loan of $14,900. The only difference is that under part II the amount of money advanced by the administration will be increased from $10,000 to $12,000.
The measure of insurance mentioned by the minister will, I think, be well received. Certainly the experience of the administration in respect of the Farm Credit Act has been satisfactory. I believe the proposal will be accorded widespread approval and a warm reception by veterans.
Further details of the amendments will be presented to the committee in due course. I merely wished to take this opportunity of making a few comments particularly because in my riding there are approximately 1,200 veterans who have taken advantage of the provisions of the Veterans' Land Act. The half acre provision that was introduced last year was well received. I know that the proposals foreshadowed by this resolution will win wholehearted support not only among the veterans and the Legion but among people all across Canada.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
Mr. Churchill thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. C-80, to amend the Veterans' Land Act.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speechtext:
Canadian Wheat Board Act points were on a seven bushel quota. It is anticipated that in a very short time all delivery points will be on an open quota basis.
This is a most remarkable change in five years. I happened to run across in Hansard for April 1957, a speech by one of those members from the province of Alberta representing the Social Credit party who drew attention to the facts in his area and I think he listed 30 or more delivery points, most of the delivery points were on the three bushel quota, some on the four bushel quota and I believe three on the five bushel delivery quota. Five years later we find almost universally across western Canada open delivery at all the delivery points.
Many of the 29 delivery points not now on an open quota have stocks of No. 1 northern wheat exclusively, and are in the Vancouver shipping area. To ship No. 1 northern from these points in excess of market requirements would cause congestion at Vancouver for a grade of wheat not in immediate market demand. However, it is anticipated that additional quantities of No. 1 northern will be required in the near future at Vancouver, and these stocks will be shipped from these 29 points. A daily check is being made on these 29 points in order that they will move to an open basis as rapidly as is possible, consistent with good marketing practices.
I have already stressed how important the stability of the wheat economy is to the prosperity of the Canadian economy in general. In achieving this stability the Canadian wheat board plays a central and vital role. This role, we all recognize, has become more difficult and complex with the growth of world surpluses and of surplus disposal programs. Consequently, the international wheat agreement, as an instrument of price stability and market guarantee, has become even more important than in the past and, in addition, our bilateral consultations with the United States have in substantial measure succeeded in safeguarding our commercial markets.
I should like to make a reference to the importance of eastern Canada as our primary commercial market for western feed grains. From time to time problems arise in the supplying of western feed grains for eastern livestock and poultry feeders. In order to bring about a closer liaison and a better understanding of these problems the Minister of Agriculture will shortly be announcing the establishment of a special eastern liaison committee ta work with the Canadian wheat board.
In closing my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I should like to re-emphasize the support of the government for the principle of western producers marketing their wheat, oats and barley through the Canadian wheat board.

Accordingly, I strongly recommend the extension of the Canadian wheat board's powers for another five years.

Mr. Speaker, at the very outset of my remarks I should like to join in the expression of regret at the absence of the Minister of Agriculture on the occasion of the presentation of this bill. I am sure all other members of the house will wish to join with me in the wish for a speedy recovery to full health on his part and an early return to participation in the activities in the House of Commons.
I must also say I was glad to hear the Minister of Veterans Affairs, who presented the bill, indicate near the end of his remarks that it was very difficult to overemphasize the importance of the stability of the wheat economy in relation to the total economy of our country. I think some of us may tend at times to underestimate the importance of the wheat economy in the over-all prosperity of the country. I was glad to hear him make that statement and I think it bears reiterating.
I do not propose to review the history of the wheat board legislation. When a similar bill was presented to parliament on February 1, 1957, the history was rather adequately reviewed by the then minister of trade and commerce, the Right Hon. C. D. Howe, as appears on page 888 of Hansard for that year. The whole history of the legislation and its development and of the changes made throughout the period since its inception are set out there, and I do not propose to repeat it.
But there are some matters in the bill that concern me a good deal and I want to address myself to them. Since the bill amends several sections of the existing act it is rather hard to describe its principle, but probably the main principle is the extension of the provisions of the act with the present powers for a further term of five years. Therefore in effect the bill renews the act

for a further term of five years although there are other important provisions in the bill.
One amendment not mentioned by the minister is the change in the definition of the word "grain" for the purpose of the act by adding rapeseed to the grains included in that designation. That is an important amendment of real substance. The development of the production of this oilseed to the present extent and the potential development in the future if proper markets can be found are quite important not only to the economy of the western provinces but to that of the whole country.
Then there is the change in the definition of the word "minister" from Minister of Trade and Commerce to Minister of Agriculture. It is a curious thing, but when that change was announced in the House of Commons taking away jurisdiction over the wheat board from the Minister of Trade and Commerce and giving it to the Minister of Agriculture no explanation was given by the government of the underlying reasons for the change. If I remember correctly, and the Minister of Veterans Affairs will bear me out in this, the change was made when he left the Department of Trade and Commerce, was moved to the portfolio of veterans affairs and the new Minister of Trade and Commerce was appointed. The new Minister of Trade and Commerce was left with a very much truncated department. Jurisdiction over wheat selling, with all its importance to the economy of the country, was taken away from him. Jurisdiction over the atomic energy control board, with all its increasing importance to this country, was taken away from him. A few other things were also taken away from him and he was left with bits and pieces of the trade and commerce department. If jurisdiction over marketing of products of our mines, the newsprint and woods industry activities was also taken away from him he would be reduced to a very junior position.
In any event, I do think that the government, having done this sort of thing, owes an explanation even at this late date as to why this change was made and why the marketing of this commodity with all its importance was taken away from the trade and commerce ministry.

Certainly some explanation is owed to the House of Commons why this change was made, and surely a change is not to be made because of the personalities of different ministers occupying the portfolio at any given time. The wheat board seems to have earned the support of the producers of grain in western Canada. I think there is virtually no opposition to it today from producers, although I can recall many debates in earlier years in this house when the spokesmen in the house for the producers opposed the wheat board rather roundly and in language that was not always a model of moderation.
There are one or two things about the bill that concern me. Apart from the change extending the act for five years, I wonder why there are so many small, relatively inconsequential amendments in the bill.
The minister spoke about marketing, increased sales, the shortage of wheat in some parts of the world, credit sales and other things. This raises in my mind one question: why was there such secrecy about the China wheat sale? Why is the house not given the relevant information about that sale, although the minister talked about other sales, the number of bushels each year and certain credit sales. So far as I am concerned, I believe that the major agreement for the China wheat sale was signed before the Minister of Agriculture left for that trip across the Pacific, and the announcement he made about having signed the agreement was completely misleading.
I asked a simple question on the order paper on this subject, and I am going to read it. The question, as it appears at page 1562 of Hansard for March 7, 1962, was:
On what date was the long term agreement between the Canadian wheat board and the China Resources Company with respect to the sale of wheat and barley signed?
2. How many individual contracts have been signed under this agreement, and what is the date of each?

Apart from the information with respect to volume and credit terms, it is contrary to government policy and not in the public interest to reveal details of the commercial sales contracts entered into by the Canadian wheat board.

I was accusing the present government of misusing it for propaganda purposes. I was going on to point out if they continue on that improper course they will damage the wheat board, damage this splendid producer organization. I also made it quite clear that it is the government who in this China wheat sale made the date of the contract such a great government secret, apparently for security purposes or some other reason of government policy. I want to point out that I believe all members of the House of Commons support efforts to sell wheat to China. They are very happy indeed about the fact this sale has been made, but they are greatly concerned about the conduct of this government in relation to that contract.
I challenge the Minister of Veterans Affairs when he replies to my remarks, as he will have an opportunity to do, to answer precisely the points I have raised. I should like to draw the attention of the house to another example of the abuse of the wheat board by the present government. In so far as the China wheat sale was concerned, the government saw fit to guarantee the payment of the wheat to the extent of $100 million. I asked some questions to obtain information about this, and I found out that the government had not used the vehicle heretofore always used for insuring payment on sales of wheat on credit terms. All previous sales had been insured under the export credits insurance legislation. The reason they could not use this legislation became quite obvious when we examined the provisions of the

measure. The $100 million was larger than the authority granted under that act, so the government could not use it.
However, there was another reason. It has been the practice, indeed it is an obligation under that act to produce and disclose such contracts. The secrecy could not, therefore, be pursued if that act had been used even if the government had increased the authority to guarantee payment under that act. In any event, I asked a question about the insuring of the contract and I received another rather long winded answer. It will be found in Hansard for February 26, 1962 at page 1246. I shall read the answer:
This matter was covered by order in council P.C. 1961-1012 of July 13, 1961, which was reported to the house in the summary of orders in council passed that month, tabled on September 27, 1961. This order authorized the Minister of Finance to give the Canadian wheat board an undertaking that, in the event of any default by the China National Cereals, Oils and Foodstuffs Import and Export Corporation in respect of payments due the board under contracts for the sale of Canadian wheat and barley made under the long term agreement between the said board and the said corporation, such parliamentary approval as may be necessary will be sought to enable direct reimbursement by the government of Canada to the board of any payments in respect of which the corporation is in default, and authorize the minister also to guarantee to six chartered banks the repayment of advances and interest thereon made to the board up to a total not to exceed $100 million outstanding at any time for the purpose of financing the sale of up to six million long tons of Canadian wheat and barley under the long term agreement between the board and the corporation.
I ask the house to note this. The second question I asked was:
If so, by what statutory authority was such guarantee or credit arrangement made?
Note this answer given by the Minister of National Defence:
The guarantee was given under section 11 of the Canadian Wheat Board Act, and the authority to make the undertaking was given to use the powers vested in the crown by section 54 of the British North America Act.
I think it will be relevant, since we sometimes in this house do not look at these things, if I read section 54 of the British North American Act. It reads:
It shall not be lawful for the House of Commons to adopt or pass any vote, resolution, address, or bill for the appropriation of any part of the public revenue, or of any tax or impost, to any purpose that has not been first recommended to that house by message of the Governor General in the session in which such vote, resolution, address, or bill is proposed.
It will be noticed, Mr. Speaker, that that section has no applicability to the subject matter at all and no relevance whatever. The answer is that in so far as the guarantee of payment of this wheat board sale, the marketing of this vast quantity of wheat,
Canadian Wheat Board Act with which, as far as I understand it, all hon. members of the house are in accord, is concerned, this section has nothing to do with it. The section says that the government has to come to the house for approval of expenditures, but once again the government did not come to the house, before making this commitment on behalf of the treasury.
The order in council is interesting. I was able to worm a copy of the order in council out of the government by having a motion of the house passed compelling its production.
I	got it, or at least a copy of it. It is not the complete copy, but I take it the original is in order, with the date it was signed. I received what purports to be a copy of it. This order in council is very interesting. It does not deal, of course, with the interest charged under this contract. That is another thing about which we can find nothing. But it does not make any reference to section
II	of the wheat board act as the authority for its passage. Of course, it is perfectly obvious why it does not. It is because section 11 of the wheat board act does not contain any such authority; it gives no such authority whatever. Therefore the government is in a position of having passed the order in council committing the taxpayers to a $100 million guarantee without the authority of parliament.
Our legislation has been very careful to give the House of Commons control over the expenditure of money, and the course for the government, a very proper one was to submit the commitment to the house for approval- I think it would have at once obtained the support of the house-and to disclose to the house relevant facts about the contract. I respectfully suggest that this is why the government did not see fit to follow the proper constitutional course and submit this guarantee by it to the house for approval in one of the three or four ways in which it could have done that. It could have done it under the export credit legislation by bringing that act in for amendment and disclosing the reason for getting the larger amount of money required; it could have done it by a simple vote in the estimates; it could have done it by an amendment to this particular bill. But before I go further, Mr. Speaker, I want to read section 11 of the wheat board act so that we will have on record just what it says. It says this:
The governor in council may authorize the Minister of Finance, on behalf of Her Majesty, to guarantee on such terms and conditions as the governor in council may approve, repayment of advances made to the board, and interest thereon, on the security of grain held by the board or otherwise, by any bank incorporated under the Bank Act for the purpose of carrying on its operations under this act, or to make loans or advances to the board on such terms and conditions as may be agreed upon.

It will be seen that nowhere there is the authority to guarantee credit to a foreign country to pay for a commodity that the foreign country is buying in Canada. It will be seen that it does not give such authority at all. It is no wonder that the order in council does not follow the usual procedure of orders in council in giving its authority in the early part of the order as drafted. The draftsman, had there been any such authority, would of course have followed the obvious practice of stating his authority right in the order in council itself.
There are two or three matters that perhaps could be pointed out in this connection. If the government is going to pursue this kind of policy in handling the wheat board, they are going to break down the wheat board and destroy confidence in it. The wheat board has developed support in this country and does at the moment enjoy the confidence and respect of those concerned with it, not only the producers of grain who are using it as their marketing agency but other people throughout the country who are concerned with the economy of the country and who attach, as the minister correctly stated, major importance to the marketing of wheat in the total economy.
It seems to me that the government should in this bill, when it is among other things correcting what it calls typographical errors in the explanatory notes-I will have some questions to ask about the typographical errors, as they are described, at the committee stage-when it is making that kind of correction it surely should have brought forward, as it was obligated by law to have done last year, an amendment that would provide the authority for this guarantee that has been given. Of course, when that is done it requires the government to disclose those parts of the transaction that are relevant to its consideration by the House of Commons. That can easily and properly be done without in any way jeopardizing those competitive parts of contracts of sale that it is not usual to disclose. There is no difficulty about the matter at all other than this abnormal and improper desire on the part of the government to conceal from this House of Commons the parts of the deal with communist China that are relevant and proper for this house to consider in this commitment of public funds to the extent of $100 million without the approval of this House of Commons.
It would seem as if here, once again, the government has, with all its record of carelessness in money matters since it took office almost five years ago, committed another grave irregularity and another failure to disclose to the house and bring before the house for its approval those matters that belong 

exclusively to the house, namely its right to approve the expenditures of public funds.
As far as that particular transaction is concerned, the interest charged, and other relevant matters, I do not doubt that the house would have approved the granting of credit on an appropriate basis or the insuring of payments to the producers on appropriate terms. I do not think there is anyone here who would have done otherwise than was done in the case of all these sales where there has been a credit risk and it has been considered advisable to sell on credit. It seems to me that this is a matter for which the government must answer.
I cannot for the life of me understand the reason for the secrecy with regard to the date of the signing of the agreement. That has always been given in the past when there have been similar agreements. As a matter of fact, there was a great fanfare when the contract was announced. There is one aspect of this which mystifies me: in answer to a question which I asked, information was volunteered which, in my opinion, would certainly be useful to competitors-for instance, the quantities to be shipped in each month up to the end of May, 1962. A shrewd commercial agent could learn a good deal from this which would be of use in bidding for further sales. As I say, I am mystified as to why the government should have given this information, which had not been requested, while refusing to give the other information concerning the rate of exchange which had been used in computing the total value of the sales-information which is relevant and necessary for a proper consideration of this matter by the House of Commons.
I am glad to say that the government agrees with the previous government that the wheat board legislation is, in general, good legislation and that it should be extended for a further term of five years, as was done a couple of days before the change of government- as a matter of fact, shortly before the dissolution of the last parliament. I would expect that after this bill has been dealt with there will be dissolution followed by a change of government in accordance with that precedent.
I am sure of that; but perhaps it is not strictly relevant to the bill we are considering, however inviting it may be to discuss the subject at this time.
I should like to ask the minister in closing whether, in addition to dealing with the points I have raised, he would give us some explanation before we reach the committee stage of the consequences of the principle of the amendment contained in clause 5 of the bill which ostensibly corrects an error in the previous act. I should like the hon. gentleman

to give the house any information which is readily available concerning the consequences of that mistake in the earlier legislation.

We are
again happy to have an opportunity of discussing one of the major Canadian marketing boards, certainly the greatest one the Canadian farmers have. In doing so, I should like to say we are unhappy that the Minister of Agriculture is not with us; we hope he makes a complete recovery and is able to return to his duties soon.
We are pleased to note the report of the minister that Canada is now in a more favourable position than for a number of years inasmuch as we have been able to reduce our surplus of wheat, a surplus which was considered to have been very large at its peak of more than 700 million bushels. Now, the minister says, we are down to a carryover of only 300 million bushels. Western farmers may be interested to learn that the minister of agriculture in Ontario, speaking about grain in Ontario the other day, pointed out that we might have been guilty of the sin of expecting that our surpluses in western Canada would continue to pile up and that we might have under-estimated the quantity which should normally be held over. He suggested that it might be necessary to hold much more grain than we have held in the past. The present situation has made it necessary, in Ontario, to buy grain; conditions have made it necessary to import grain, and eastern agriculture is looking with some reservations upon the limiting of the surpluses which were considered inevitable for a long time to come. I think we may find that in the next year or two there may have to be an increase in production in those areas which are capable of increased production. We may find ourselves in the happy position of producing more wheat, since the government is going to sell that wheat.
I, personally, would like to congratulate the government on the amount of wheat it has sold. I do this indirectly because, really, it is the wheat board itself that we are congratulating. A member of this committee interrupted another hon. member a few moments ago to point out that the government was not controlling the wheat board. That is true. It is a credit to the wheat board organization and its directors, a credit to the western farmer and, I think, a credit to the governments of Canada, whether this one or previous governments, that we should now have reached a stage after 25 years at which the wheat board itself is capable of going across the world, making advantageous sales and getting co-operation from the administration to allow it to receive currency which the
Canadian Wheat Board Act trading nations are able to tender. I think that is a very good thing. The wheat board has over the years developed to a point at which it commands a great deal of respect. It has also undertaken a great deal of responsibility.
I think it would not be out of place to draw attention to some of the advances made by the Canadian wheat board in the 25 years of its existence. As we all know, this is a government marketing agency. It is an agency established by parliament to market on a national and international basis all the grains specified in the act. When the Minister of Veterans Affairs announced the other day that we had participated with 57 countries across the world in establishing a new international wheat agreement, he was, I think, indicating to everyone in this country that here was a national marketing board which had come of age and which was now a prime factor in the agricultural economy of Canada. In the light of this I cannot but wonder how the members of parliament, a week or two ago, could have taken the action they did in this house and made the references they did in relation to all the national marketing boards.
This is the only major one we have tried and it has been successful. This is a socialistic type of marketing board. There are 230,000 grain producers belonging to it. Each gave up a certain amount of the free enterprise spirit to operate under the quota system which in the short term on many occasions has proved not to be advantageous. It has been argued that because of the quota system, because of the international wheat agreement and because a long term agreement had to be worked out by the board the farmer in one year may not have received as much as he hoped to receive. The farmers have to regulate themselves to a large extent by establishing quotas of production. That is essential under any marketing board we establish. Those who belong must realize they have to put something in in order to take something out. I believe the farmers of western Canada deserve to be congratulated for co-operating among themselves in establishing the board and making it successful.
I would be remiss if I did not on this occasion congratulate the present hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale as well as the former member for that riding. Since coming to the house I have heard much talk about rapeseed and have concluded it must be important in that area. Before the present hon. member from that constituency was elected to this house the previous representative also talked about the importance of rapeseed.

In the highly competitive international wheat market of today, any price reduction offered to gain a temporary advantage over a competing exporter will almost certainly set the ceiling for subsequent sales. These are only a few of the many factors which go into the daily pricing of Canadian wheat. It is a fact that the price the wheat board has maintained is much higher than prices prevailing during any other period of big surpluses.
Admittedly, the price of wheat is not high enough to compensate the western farmer for his present high costs. But, without the wheat board as a single selling agency, there is no doubt that the price would be much lower and the farmer in much greater trouble.
I believe that the history of the Canadian wheat board has been sufficiently important that it should be supported not only in western Canada but also in eastern Canada. Not only do I believe that it should be supported, Mr. Speaker, but I believe that a leaf should be taken out of its book, where with 25 years of experience the operations of a national marketing board have been successful, and that we should establish for all commodities this type of legislation.
The Canadian wheat board has certainly set a pattern. I hope I am wrong in assuming that there are some resentments against this type of co-operative enterprise on the part of primary producers themselves. Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words on this Bill No. C-75, an act to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act.
Those of us who are from the eastern part of the country have many things to say about this bill. This evening, however, I will limit myself to a few comments on the feed grain market, with which eastern Canada is especially concerned.
In my opinion, this market, which constitutes an asset for eastern Canada, should be protected, representing as it does some 100 million bushels of feed grain.
Last year we suffered from a shortage of grain following the regulation imposed by the Canadian wheat board which had stored grain for export in eastern warehouses. Now, this grain shortage caused a substantial increase not only in the price of grain but also in the transportation costs of the grain which came to us by rail instead of by boat. The price of grain increased so much that the production of hogs and chickens was reduced and the eastern farmers suffered real hardship.
I believe that the best market we have for feed grain is the domestic market. The government cannot protect this market because it has no long term policy in this regard, only a day-to-day policy. It is somewhat like the dairy industry policy. We have surpluses, while we lack grain to feed our cattle.
Canadian Wheat Board Act
I should have liked to quote figures to show what damage this government is causing to our eastern farmers, but unfortunately I do not have my notes with me. I shall soon have the opportunity, no doubt, of coming back on this subject to prove that the present government's policy concerning the feed grain market is harmful to our farmers.
I have another criticism to make about the government's grain policy. It has to do with transportation. There is a grain transportation subsidy policy which we mean to keep-

On many occasions grain dealers and farmers in the east have held meetings following which recommendations were made to the government. In particular, they made one which was not accepted, and that was the one concerning the appointment of a commissioner from the east to the Canadian wheat board. I was given the answer that the two commissioners who resigned since 1957 were not replaced by a representative from eastern Canada, although the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hamilton) had promised last year that a representative from eastern Canada would be appointed to the Canadian wheat board.

Mr. Speaker, I am not talking about the transportation of grain but about the appointment of a commissioner who would look after the distribution, in an adequate manner, in eastern Canada. A commissioner could make suggestions to the government with regard to the distribution of grain, regulate the stocks in eastern silos, as well as the transportation of western grain to the east.
We know that the free market that exists in the United States is a threat to or a handicap for the eastern farmer. In the United States, the grain market is free, which enables the American farmer to pay a price much lower than the one the eastern farmer has to pay, and then to come and compete with our products on the eastern markets.
Thus, we noticed, last year, a considerable increase in imports from the United States, due to the lower costs of the American farmer compared to that of the Canadian farmer.
The policy of the present government has impoverished the eastern farmer to such an extent that he can no longer make a profit in stock-breeding. Furthermore, the large companies are going in for integration and want to replace the farmer.
Today, we can notice that the farmer in eastern Canada goes in for stock-breeding on a limited scale. Hog-breeding and broiler chicken-farming are affected to a large extent, and there is even today integrated breeding of slaughterhouse cattle.

Mr. Speaker, the only conclusion that can be drawn is that the policy of the Conservative government needs to be revised, not only to protect the eastern farmer, but also to prevent the exodus of the farmers who, every year, swell the ranks of the unemployed.

Mr. Speaker, the bill before the house I am sure will receive general approval from all parts of the house since its main provision is to extend the life of the Canadian wheat board for a further period of five years. This is the type of orderly marketing system that has been built up over the years with the support of western producers and the approval of the parliament of Canada. This is a compulsory system for the marketing of grain, but it has the support of the overwhelming majority of western producers. In order to substantiate this statement, Mr. Speaker, I need only point out what whenever farm organizations have discussed the Canadian wheat board they have gone on record as supporting the Canadian wheat board and, further, they have gone on record in asking that the provisions of the act be extended.
The operations of the Canadian wheat board are provided for in the Canadian

Wheat Board Act, but the whole cost of the operation and maintenance of the wheat board is paid by the grain producers out of the sale price of the commodities handled by the Canadian wheat board on their behalf. From time to time, as further payments are announced by the minister in charge, it is sometimes felt that these payments come out of the federal treasury. When the cost of maintaining and operating the wheat board is discussed sometimes it is felt, and it is said, that these costs are paid out of the federal treasury.
The fact of the matter is that all of the operating costs of the Canadian wheat board are borne by the producers themselves, even pensions provided for the Canadian wheat board as well as their salaries. This is clearly demonstrated in the bill now before us, which provides for a further expense to the producers by providing for group life insurance plans and group medical plans for the employees of the wheat board. I am sure that this is the kind of provision that would recommend itself to the producers, but it demonstrates again that the producers are paying the whole of the operating costs of the wheat board.
Very often I think the producers themselves do not understand the efficiency of the wheat board's operation. When the wheat board has come before the agriculture committee of this House of Commons they have been able to demonstrate time after time that their operations are exceedingly efficient. As a matter of fact the total administrative costs of the Canadian wheat board have over the years been under one cent per bushel of grain handled. I think this is a very clear demonstration of the great efficiency of the wheat board.
There are some very large costs attached to the operations of the board for which the board pays the bill. These are the operating costs of the elevators, the storage and handling costs; but the cost of the wheat board machinery itself is less than a cent a bushel. I think that producers generally are most happy to be able to pay this very small charge and to receive the great benefits that flow from this central pooling operation and the control that flows under this act.
Mr. Speaker, there is what I call a small amendment; not that it is not an important one, but it is small in relation to the whole operation of the board, namely to include in the definition section the word "rapeseed". I would suggest that the government should have made the provision for the inclusion of mustard seed. As the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale said-I think we should shorten that constituency to "H.M.T."
Business of the House
because these names are getting rather cumbersome-"To make it effective you would have to amend some other acts". But surely that is no reason for not starting with this act; and then to make the provision for mustard seed fully effective it is necessary to amend other acts. Then the government can proceed in a regular fashion by amending the other complementary acts so that the full effect of providing for the addition of mustard seed in the Canadian Wheat Board Act would be brought about.
In recent weeks the Canadian wheat board has demonstrated the contribution it can make to orderly marketing in Canada and to the orderly marketing of grain in the world markets. The Canadian wheat board was represented at the international wheat council which discussed and made provision for a further international wheat agreement. While wheat agreements may from time to time not have within them all the provisions that some of us would wish, nevertheless this is the kind of further extension of the system of orderly marketing that commends itself to the western grain producers, and I believe will commend itself to the parliament of Canada.
Some improvements in the international wheat agreement have been obtained in part by the good work of the Canadian wheat board representation at that conference; but, Mr. Speaker, these concessions were in my judgment of a modest type. Initially they hoped to get an increase in the maximum world price of 25 cents a bushel. I think there are arguments why the increase [DOT] should be more. They had to settle for an increase of only 121 cents. Part of the reason, I think, for this concession, or this moderate settlement, was the fact that emerging nations have put forward a case for grain prices as low as possible. I think there is a great deal to the suggestion that in the marketing of grain in the world today there should be a clear division between commercial sales and sales of a non-commercial nature and that we should now have two types of international agreement, one to provide for commercial sales and another to provide for an orderly manner of distribution of grain in the non-commercial markets of the world. If this were done, then I suggest it might well be possible to get the kind of increase in the price of wheat for which producers have been hoping for many years.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it ten o'clock.
